title: Sisney v. Reisch
lead: A prison settlement promised kosher meals to a defined class of inmates, and an inmate outside the original suit sought to enforce that promise.

actors.name: Heftel
actors.role: Inmate who obtained the religious-diet settlement

actors.name: Bloomberg
actors.role: Corrections secretary who signed the settlement

actors.name: Reisch and Weber
actors.role: Current corrections secretary and prison-operations director sued by Sisney

actors.name: CBM
actors.role: Prison food provider that changed the meals

proceedings: Circuit court: dismissed for immunity and insufficient allegations of official responsibility.
South Dakota Supreme Court: reversed and remanded unanimously.
limits: The existing complaint stated contractual and declaratory claims; breach, food compliance, and ultimate liability remained unresolved. Leave to amend was not reached.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Heftel’s settlement promises meals beyond his own plate
sections.cue: Introduce the agreement before the later inmate’s claim.
paragraphs: In 1998, an inmate named Heftel sued the Department of Corrections under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, alleging interference with his free exercise of Judaism. In February 2000, Heftel and then-corrections secretary Bloomberg signed a settlement promising a kosher diet to all Jewish inmates who requested it. The agreement specified prepackaged certified kosher meals at noon and evening. It extended the diet regardless of custody status and included meals before and after fast days.

Sisney later alleged that he was Jewish and requested that diet. In February 2007, prison food provider CBM stopped supplying prepackaged meals and served a new diet that included rice and beans prepared in the prison kitchen. Sisney claimed the change violated both the settlement and his religious requirements.

sections.title: Officials reject the grievance and the complaint is dismissed
sections.cue: Trace the pleaded responsibility of the defendants.
paragraphs: When Sisney grieved the change, prison-operations director Weber responded that Sisney was not a party to the settlement. Sisney sued Weber and current corrections secretary Reisch in official and individual capacities. The circuit court dismissed on immunity grounds and because it found insufficient allegations that these officials were responsible for carrying out the settlement. It did not reach beneficiary status. Sisney appealed both dismissal and the absence of an opportunity to amend.

The South Dakota Supreme Court reviewed de novo, looking favorably at factual assertions while requiring circumstances supporting more than speculative relief. Reisch occupied the office of the secretary who had signed for the department, and statutes placed the penitentiary under the department’s direction and secretary’s administration. Weber’s alleged operational role also supported an inference of responsibility. The complaint did not have to conclusively establish liability at this stage.

sections.title: The promise expressly identifies the class that includes Sisney
sections.cue: Explain the beneficiary ruling without assuming breach.
paragraphs: Under South Dakota Codified Laws § 53-2-6, a contract expressly benefiting a third person could be enforced before rescission. That person need not supply consideration or be owed a preexisting duty by the promisee. Clear contractual intent could supply the necessary privity, and could identify a class without listing each member by name.

This settlement expressly promised performance to all Jewish inmates requesting kosher meals. Its provisions about custody status and fast days reinforced that intended class benefit, beyond an incidental consequence of prison administration. Sisney alleged membership in the class. He therefore stated a third-party beneficiary claim despite not signing the settlement or joining Heftel’s suit. That established a sufficient pleading, not a finding that the new food breached the agreement.

sections.title: The State’s contractual undertaking answers the immunity defense
sections.cue: Keep contractual enforcement and declaratory relief distinct.
paragraphs: The officials invoked statutes protecting against liability for inadequate prison services and injuries arising from prison-administered programs or services. The court recognized that official-capacity claims were effectively against the State and that individual immunity could depend on a discretionary-ministerial distinction. It assumed possible general immunity without deciding those classifications.

The decisive point was contractual waiver: by entering a contract, the State waived immunity to the extent a party or intended beneficiary sought enforcement of its undertaking. The cited South Dakota decisions did not immunize contractual liability merely because the underlying operation was governmental or proprietary. The officials argued that Sisney had forfeited the immunity issue by failing to brief it, but he had argued that mandatory meal performance was ministerial. The contract ground made it unnecessary to decide that characterization.

Sisney also requested a declaration. The invoked statutes addressed imposing liability and did not generally preclude declaratory relief from an invalid act or abuse of official authority. He could pursue that remedy as well. The ruling did not abolish immunity for unrelated torts or establish that any claim labeled declaratory necessarily escaped it.

sections.title: The existing complaint returns to the circuit court
sections.cue: State the judgment and why the companion case differs.
paragraphs: Justice Zinter wrote for a unanimous five-member court. It reversed and remanded, with Chief Justice Gilbertson and Justices Sabers, Konenkamp, and Meierhenry concurring. Because the existing complaint was sufficient, it did not address leave to amend.

The separate same-day decision in Sisney v. State concerned CBM’s general food-service agreement with the State. This case concerned a settlement expressly promising meals to an identified class that included Sisney. The difference was the particular undertaking, not a universal rule that inmates could always, or never, enforce government contracts. No post-remand liability determination was made here.
